tier_reason: The only numbers against QEMU are a March 2022 blog post by the Box86/Box64 author (a competing project), read here from search snippets because box86.org is blocked; the CPU model, compiler flags and emulator versions are not visible, and it is not a well-known independent suite, so it falls short of A and B. FEX itself publishes no numbers against QEMU.

corrections.claimed_speedup: x86_64 guest, FEX against QEMU: 7z 1486 vs 931 (1.6x, derived from page data); dav1d 1 thread 27.28 vs 11.24 (2.4x, derived from page data). x86 guest: 7z 1197 vs 691 (1.7x, derived from page data); dav1d 1 thread 21.75 vs 10.57 (2.1x, derived from page data). Box64 in the same table: 7z 3084, dav1d 1 thread 49.72 (Box86: 3117 and 49.94). The article's summary puts FEX at 13-26% of native speed on 7-Zip and dav1d, against QEMU at 5-16% and Box64 at 27-53%. The record's other x86_64 figures (dav1d 4 threads 52.67 vs 15.65, glmark2 164 vs 4, OpenArena 1.8 vs 0.083) could not be confirmed here.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 8.2k stars, 380 forks. In discussion #4113 the maintainer said in October 2024 that FEX does not support Android, and a July 2026 comment says the Chinese Android app Game Fusion uses FEX. An HN snippet says Valve funds Igalia work on FEX for its Snapdragon-based Steam Frame headset (snippet only).
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: box86.org is blocked here, so the numbers were read from search-result text. Search snippets confirm the 7z and dav1d 1-thread rows for both guests; the dav1d 4-thread, glmark2 and OpenArena x86_64 figures could not be checked. The CPU model, compiler flags and the QEMU and FEX versions are not visible. The measurement is from March 2022 and was made by the Box86/Box64 author, a competing project; FEX has changed a lot since, and its maintainer said in October 2024 (discussion #4113) that he has never compared FEX with Box and that its CPU emulation performance has improved over the years. The glmark2 and OpenArena gaps mostly measure GL forwarding, not the JIT: the article says QEMU has no GL pass-through by default and renders in software. An HN snippet says FEX was slower than QEMU on some workloads and had glitches (snippet only, no numbers). FEX publishes no numbers of its own against QEMU in its README. In these tables FEX is slower than Box64 on every row.

notes: Kept at C: real comparison against QEMU user-mode, but from a competitor's 2022 blog with unknown hardware and versions; box86.org (benchmark_url) and brianlovin.com (HN mirror) were EGRESS_BLOCKED, so only snippets were seen. Shortcomings to record: competitor-run and 4 years old, methodology unknown, slower than Box64 on every row, GL rows measure GL forwarding against QEMU's software rendering, dav1d 4-thread/glmark2/OpenArena figures unconfirmed. Metadata confirmed: MIT, 8.2k stars, last commit 2026-10-05, active.

tier_reason: No published speed claim for tpy's output against CPython: the README has none, and the only CPython ratio in the repo (a TODO.md developer note, '7.6x vs CPython') is for hand-edited generated C++, not compiler output. Developer notes against Shed Skin show tpy slower or level, so no number supports a win over the baseline.

corrections.workload: No published benchmark of tpy output against CPython. Developer notes in TODO.md (measured 2026-10-05) time Shed Skin's sieve and ant example programs under tpy and Shed Skin, and a JSON parse of a 15 MB, 20K-record dataset; scripts/perf/generator_frames.py compares generator forms inside tpy only.
corrections.claimed_speedup: No speed claim against CPython for compiler output. TODO.md developer notes: a JSON parser written in tpy went from 68 ms to 59 ms after library changes, and hand-optimized generated C++ (checked arithmetic removed, direct indexing) reached 23 ms, '7.6x vs CPython' (that ratio is for hand-edited C++; it implies roughly 175 ms for CPython and about 3x for the 59 ms compiler output, derived from page data with rounded inputs, and the note does not say whether CPython ran the same parser or the json module). Against Shed Skin, tpy is slower or level: sieve 1.14 s vs Shed Skin 0.66 s (0.69 s only with GLIBC malloc tunables), ant 2.87 s vs 2.58 s (Shed Skin with Boost flat map) and 3.30 s (Shed Skin with standard containers). RELEASE_NOTES.md: generator changes up to 2x faster than the previous tpy release on consumer-heavy loops.
corrections.caveats: Early development, pre-1.0: the README says 'known bugs can produce wrong results silently' and BUGS.md (about 2.3 MB) lists many open items, including a hang where CPython finishes in 0.158 s. No published speed evidence against CPython, so tier D with very low notability (6 stars, 0 forks; the tpy-examples repo has 1 star). TODO.md holds internal developer timings only: the one CPython ratio (7.6x) is for hand-edited generated C++, and against Shed Skin tpy is 1.7x slower on sieve without malloc tunables and between Shed Skin's two builds on ant; no hardware or compiler flags are given for these. tpy-lang.org (docs) is blocked here and was not checked. Name collision: the PyPI package 'turbopython' is a different project (ribalba/TurboPython, version 0.1.0, uploaded 2026-03-11) whose description claims 37.1x and 59.4x over pure Python; those numbers do not belong to trozen/tpy-lang.
